title: DTF Transfer File Preparation
seoTitle: DTF Transfer File Preparation Guide — Gang Sheets, White Underbase, and Gang Layout
seoDescription: Prepare artwork for DTF printing with proper white underbase, transparent backgrounds, gang sheet layout, and cut contours. No white boxes, clean separations.
content:
# DTF Transfer File Preparation

DTF (Direct-to-Film) printing requires specific file prep: a transparent background so the white underbase layer only prints where ink sits, proper color management, and gang sheet layout that maximizes film use. This guide covers the full production sequence from customer artwork to press-ready transfers.

## Why Vectorr for DTF?

Transparent Backgrounds: Convert any source image to PNG with true alpha transparency—no white boxes.

White Underbase Preview: See exactly where white ink will print before you send the file to the RIP.

Gang Sheet Layout Tools: Nest multiple designs on one sheet with automatic spacing and rotation.

## DTF File Requirements

1. **Format**: PNG with alpha channel, or PDF with transparent background. JPG cannot be transparent.
2. **Resolution**: 300 PPI at final print size. Upscaling after the fact adds softness.
3. **Color Mode**: RGB (DTF printers convert to CMYK + White internally).
4. **White Underbase**: Automatically generated by the RIP based on opacity. Semi-transparent pixels get partial white.

## Gang Sheet Workflow

1. **Collect Orders**: Group all jobs for one production run.
2. **Standardize Sizes**: Resize each design to final print dimensions.
3. **Nest on Sheet**: Arrange designs to minimize waste, leaving 3–5mm gutter between each.
4. **Add Cut Contours**: Draw a path around each design (2mm offset) if using a contour cutter.
5. **Export**: Full-resolution PNG or PDF, one file per gang sheet.

## Common DTF Pitfalls

White Box Around Design: The source file had a white background instead of transparency. Re-export with alpha channel enabled, or use Vectorr's background removal.

Soft Edges: Source image was upscaled after tracing. Always vectorize at the target resolution.

Color Shift: RGB values change when printed. Use an ICC profile in your RIP that matches your specific DTF printer and powder type.

Peeling After Wash: Underbase too thin (increase white ink density in RIP), or press temperature/time incorrect.

## Gang Sheet Layout Strategy

DTF film is billed by length, so efficient nesting saves money. Standard widths are 13", 22", or 24". Small designs (under 4" × 4") should rotate to fit gaps. Leave consistent gutter (3–5mm) so the cutter doesn't clip adjacent designs. Keep a 10mm safe margin from sheet edges to avoid print-head strikes.

## White Underbase and Opacity

The RIP generates white underbase automatically wherever colored pixels sit. Opacity drives coverage: 100% opacity = full white, 50% opacity = half coverage. Semi-transparent edges (from anti-aliasing) get partial white, which produces a soft halo on dark garments. For crisp edges, sharpen transparency with a levels adjustment before export.

## Cut Contour Setup

If using a contour cutter (e.g., SummaCut, Graphtec), add a spot-color path named "CutContour" on a separate layer. Offset the path 1–2mm outside the artwork. The RIP will print this as a registration mark for the cutter. Without a contour, you hand-cut each transfer, which is slow for production runs.

## File Naming for Production

Use a consistent naming scheme: `OrderNumber_CustomerName_Size.png`. This lets you trace each transfer back to its order. For gang sheets, name the file by production date: `GangSheet_2026-11-06_Sheet1.png`.

## Color Management

DTF printers are not calibrated like offset presses. Colors shift between printers, powder types, and press times. The only reliable preview is a test print on the actual substrate. Build an ICC profile from test swatches, then apply it in the RIP before printing production runs.

## Troubleshooting

If white shows through colored areas, the RIP's underbase choke is too wide—reduce it by 0.5mm. If colors look washed out, increase white ink density. If the transfer cracks when stretched, the film cure time was too short or the press temperature too high.

title: Screen Print Color Separation
seoTitle: Screen Print Color Separation Guide — Spot Colors, Underbase, and Halftones
seoDescription: Separate spot colors for screen printing with proper underbase layers, halftone angles, registration marks, and color count optimization for cost efficiency.
content:
# Screen Print Color Separation

Screen printing requires artwork broken into individual spot colors, each printed as a separate screen. Proper separation determines print quality, registration accuracy, and production cost. This guide covers the full workflow from artwork to press-ready films.

## Why Vectorr for Screen Printing?

Spot Color Assignment: Convert full-color artwork to Pantone swatches with automatic color reduction.

Underbase Layer Generation: Calculate white underbase coverage for dark garments automatically.

Registration Mark Placement: Add crop marks and color bars to every separation for accurate screen alignment.

## Separation Requirements

1. **Color Mode**: Spot colors (Pantone), not CMYK process. Each color = one screen.
2. **Resolution**: 300 PPI for halftones, vector preferred for solid areas.
3. **Underbase**: White ink printed first on dark garments, blocks fabric color from showing through.
4. **Registration Marks**: Crosshairs outside print area, printed on every screen for alignment.

## Color Separation Workflow

1. **Analyze Artwork**: Count distinct colors. Gradients require halftones.
2. **Reduce Colors**: Merge similar shades to minimize screen count (4-color max for manual presses, 6-8 for automatics).
3. **Assign Pantone**: Match each color to a Pantone swatch for ink mixing.
4. **Create Underbase**: Generate white layer that covers all colored areas on dark garments. Choke it 0.5-1mm to prevent halo.
5. **Set Halftone Angles**: Use 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 0° to avoid moiré patterns between overlapping screens.
6. **Add Registration**: Place crosshair marks 10mm outside print boundary, same position on every separation.

## Underbase Strategy

**Light Garments**: No underbase needed if fabric is white or pastel.

**Dark Garments**: Full white underbase under all colors. Print underbase first, flash cure, then print colors on top.

**Choke the Underbase**: Make it 0.5-1mm smaller than the color layers so white doesn't peek out at edges.

**Selective Underbase**: For designs with large solid areas, only underbase the colored regions to save ink and prevent stiffness.

## Halftone Considerations

**Line Screen**: 45-55 LPI for manual presses, 65-85 LPI for automatics. Higher LPI = finer detail but harder to print.

**Dot Shape**: Round dots for general use, elliptical for smooth gradients.

**Angle Assignment**: Each color needs a unique angle to prevent moiré. Standard angles: C=22.5°, M=75°, Y=0°, K=45°.

**Minimum Dot**: 5% for manual presses, 3% for automatics. Smaller dots wash out during exposure.

## Color Count Optimization

Each screen adds setup time and cost. Reduce colors without sacrificing quality:

- Merge similar shades (navy + royal blue → single blue).
- Use overprinting: print cyan over yellow to create green instead of a separate green screen.
- Consolidate small details into the darkest color.
- Eliminate outlier colors that appear in <5% of the design.

## Registration Marks

**Crosshairs**: Two perpendicular lines forming a + symbol, 3-5mm long.

**Placement**: Minimum 10mm outside the print boundary, same position on every color.

**Color Bars**: Small squares of each spot color printed outside the image area for ink density verification.

## Output Specifications

**Film Positives**: One black film per color, printed at 1200-3000 DPI. Black areas block UV light during screen exposure.

**Film Orientation**: Emulsion side down (ink side touches the screen during exposure).

**Screen Mesh**: 110-160 mesh for general printing, 200-230 for fine halftones, 60-86 for opaque white underbase.

## Common Separation Errors

**Moiré Patterns**: Overlapping halftones at the same angle create visible interference. Use proper angle separation (15-30° between each color).

**Registration Drift**: Screens misalign during printing. Add trap (0.25-0.5mm overlap) between adjacent colors to hide gaps.

**White Halo**: Underbase extends beyond color layers. Choke the underbase by 0.5-1mm.

**Lost Detail**: Halftone dots too small for the mesh count. Use coarser LPI or higher mesh count.

title: Sublimation Print File Preparation
seoTitle: Sublimation Print Preparation — Mirroring, Color Management, and Bleed for Polyester
seoDescription: Prepare files for dye sublimation printing on polyester with proper mirroring for hard goods, color management for substrate shifts, and bleed requirements.
content:
# Sublimation Print File Preparation

Dye sublimation transfers ink into polyester fibers using heat and pressure. The process requires polyester or polymer-coated substrates, mirrored artwork for hard goods, and color management to account for substrate tone shifts. This guide covers file prep from artwork to heat press.

## Why Vectorr for Sublimation?

Automatic Mirroring: Flip designs for hard goods (mugs, phone cases, tiles) with one click.

Color Profile Management: Preview how colors shift on different polyester substrates before printing.

Bleed Extension: Automatically expand artwork beyond trim line to eliminate white edges.

## Sublimation Requirements

1. **Substrate**: Polyester fabric (100% polyester best, 65% minimum) or polymer-coated hard goods (mugs, tiles, metal sheets).
2. **Color Mode**: RGB (sublimation inks are RGB-based, not CMYK).
3. **Resolution**: 300 PPI at final size. Sublimation reveals pixelation more than other print methods.
4. **Mirroring**: Required for hard goods (mugs, tiles, phone cases). Not needed for direct-to-fabric printing.

## Why Polyester Only?

Sublimation ink becomes gas under heat and bonds with polyester molecules. Cotton, linen, and other natural fibers cannot hold sublimation dye — the color washes out immediately. For blended fabrics, only the polyester portion holds color (65/35 poly-cotton appears faded compared to 100% poly).

## Mirroring Workflow

**Direct-to-Fabric (Apparel)**: Print normally, no mirroring. Transfer paper sits face-down on fabric during pressing.

**Hard Goods (Mugs, Tiles, Phone Cases)**: Mirror the design horizontally before printing. The printed side wraps around the substrate, so the image must be reversed to read correctly after transfer.

**Text-Heavy Designs**: Double-check mirroring. Text must read backward on the transfer paper to read forward on the finished product.

## Color Management

Sublimation produces brighter, more saturated colors than other print methods, but final color depends on substrate tone:

**White Polyester**: Brightest colors, full gamut. Design as printed.

**Light Gray or Off-White**: Colors shift cooler and less vibrant. Increase saturation 10-15% in source file.

**Colored Substrates**: Sublimation has no white ink — the substrate color shows through. Printing yellow on blue poly yields green. Use white or light substrates only.

**Dark Polyester**: Sublimation doesn't work. Dye cannot lighten a dark base. Use white or light substrates exclusively.

## Bleed Requirements

Sublimation transfers often shift slightly during heat pressing. Add bleed to prevent white edges:

**Apparel**: 6-10mm bleed beyond trim line on all sides.

**Hard Goods**: Wrap artwork around edges by 3-5mm. For mugs, extend design 5mm past the seam.

**Full-Bleed Designs**: Expand background or pattern outward rather than scaling the entire design (which distorts proportions).

## ICC Profiles and Color Accuracy

Every sublimation printer + ink + paper + substrate combination produces different color. Use ICC profiles to match screen preview to printed output:

1. **Obtain Profile**: Download from your paper manufacturer (e.g., Texprint, Neenah, A-Sub) or create a custom profile using a colorimeter.
2. **Assign Profile**: Load into your RIP software or printer driver.
3. **Soft Proof**: Preview the file with the profile applied to see color shifts before printing.
4. **Test Print**: Always run a small test swatch before full production.

## Temperature and Time Settings

Sublimation is heat-activated. Too low = pale colors; too high = scorching or color shift:

**Polyester Fabric**: 385-400°F, 45-60 seconds, medium-heavy pressure.

**Mugs**: 380-400°F, 180-240 seconds, mug press.

**Hard Substrates (tiles, metal)**: 375-400°F, 60-90 seconds, firm pressure.

## Common Sublimation Mistakes

**White Edges**: Insufficient bleed or transfer shifted during pressing. Add 6-10mm bleed.

**Faded Colors**: Transfer temperature too low, pressure too light, or substrate polyester content below 65%. Increase heat or use 100% polyester.

**Ghosting**: Transfer moved during pressing. Use heat-resistant tape to secure transfer to substrate.

**Yellow Cast**: Over-pressing (too hot or too long) scorches the polyester. Lower temp or reduce time.

**Color Mismatch**: No ICC profile applied. Sublimation colors are significantly brighter than screen RGB — use a profile for accurate preview.

faqs.question: Why does sublimation only work on polyester?
faqs.answer: Sublimation ink bonds at the molecular level with polyester. Natural fibers like cotton cannot hold the dye — it washes out. For blends, only the polyester portion holds color, so 65/35 poly-cotton looks faded.

faqs.question: When do I need to mirror my sublimation design?
faqs.answer: Mirror for hard goods (mugs, tiles, phone cases, metal sheets) because the printed side wraps around the substrate. Don't mirror for direct-to-fabric apparel printing.

faqs.question: What causes white edges on sublimation prints?
faqs.answer: Insufficient bleed or the transfer shifted during pressing. Add 6-10mm bleed beyond trim line and use heat-resistant tape to secure the transfer.

faqs.question: Can I sublimate on dark polyester?
faqs.answer: No. Sublimation has no white ink and cannot lighten a dark base. Use white or light-colored polyester only. The substrate color shows through transparent areas.

faqs.question: How do I match sublimation colors to my screen?
faqs.answer: Use an ICC profile specific to your printer, ink, paper, and substrate combination. Sublimation produces brighter colors than screen RGB, so soft proofing with a profile is essential for accuracy.

title: UV Flatbed Print File Setup
seoTitle: UV Flatbed Printing File Setup — CMYK+W, White Underbase, and Spot Varnish
seoDescription: Prepare files for UV flatbed printing with white channel for transparent materials, spot varnish layer, and material-specific color profiles.
content:
# UV Flatbed Print File Setup

UV flatbed printers use UV-cured inks to print directly onto rigid materials (acrylic, wood, metal, glass). The white ink channel allows printing on transparent or dark substrates, and spot varnish adds gloss or texture. This guide covers file prep from artwork to material-specific output.

## Why Vectorr for UV Printing?

White Channel Preview: See exactly where white ink prints before sending to the RIP.

Spot Varnish Layer: Assign varnish to specific areas (text, logos, textures) as a separate channel.

Material Profiles: Load ICC profiles for acrylic, wood, metal, glass to preview color shifts per substrate.

## UV Print Requirements

1. **Color Mode**: CMYK + White (5-color or 6-color with light cyan/magenta). Some printers add Clear for spot varnish.
2. **Resolution**: 600-1200 DPI for photographic quality, 300-600 DPI for signage.
3. **White Ink Channel**: Required for transparent substrates (clear acrylic, glass) or dark materials (black aluminum, walnut).
4. **Spot Varnish**: Optional clear coat applied to specific areas for gloss, matte, or texture effects.

## White Ink Strategy

**Transparent Materials (clear acrylic, glass)**: Print white first as a full underbase, then CMYK on top. White blocks the background from showing through.

**Dark Materials (black metal, dark wood)**: Print white underbase only where CMYK sits to save ink and prevent cracking. Choke white 0.5mm to avoid halo.

**Light Materials (white aluminum, birch plywood)**: Skip white entirely unless design includes light pastels that need opacity boost.

**Flood White vs Spot White**: Flood = full white rectangle under entire design. Spot = white only where needed (saves ink, prevents cracking on flexible materials).

## Spot Varnish Workflow

Spot varnish (clear coat) adds gloss, texture, or matte finish to specific areas:

1. **Create Varnish Layer**: Duplicate the artwork layer, convert to grayscale.
2. **Define Varnish Areas**: Black = full varnish, gray = partial, white = no varnish. Use selections to isolate text, logos, or textures.
3. **Assign to Clear Channel**: Save varnish layer as a spot color named "Varnish" or "Clear" (RIP software maps this to the varnish channel).
4. **Layering**: Varnish prints last (after CMYK + White). For raised texture, print multiple varnish passes.

## Material-Specific Settings

**Acrylic (clear or white)**: Print white first on back side for reverse-mount applications. Use second-surface printing to protect CMYK from scratches.

**Wood (birch, walnut, bamboo)**: Grain absorbs ink unevenly. Increase ink density 10-15% and use wood-specific ICC profile.

**Metal (aluminum, stainless)**: Requires primer or white underbase for color adhesion. Anodized aluminum holds UV ink directly.

**Glass**: White underbase mandatory. Print in reverse for second-surface applications (ink sits between glass and white layer).

**Textured Surfaces**: Increase ink laydown and reduce print speed. Use white underbase to fill texture and create smooth color surface.

## Color Management

UV inks appear different on each material. Use ICC profiles to match screen preview to printed output:

**White Substrates (white acrylic, birch)**: Colors print close to screen RGB. Use standard CMYK profile.

**Transparent Substrates (clear acrylic, glass)**: White underbase color affects final tone. Use profile designed for white-backed CMYK.

**Dark Substrates (black aluminum, walnut)**: White underbase brightness determines color vibrancy. Test white density before production run.

## Common UV Printing Issues

**Ink Cracking**: Too much white ink on flexible materials. Reduce white density or use spot white instead of flood white.

**Color Shift**: No material-specific ICC profile applied. Wood, metal, and acrylic all require different profiles.

**Poor Adhesion**: Material not prepped correctly. Some substrates need primer, flame treatment, or degreasing before printing.

**White Halo**: White underbase extends beyond CMYK edges. Choke white 0.5mm or use trapping in the RIP.

**Varnish Streaks**: Nozzle clog in clear channel. Run cleaning cycle before production.

## File Output Specifications

**Format**: PDF with spot colors for white and varnish channels, or multi-page TIFF (one page per channel: CMYK, White, Varnish).

**Color Space**: CMYK for color channels, grayscale for white and varnish.

**Bleed**: 3-5mm beyond trim line for edge-to-edge prints.

**Resolution**: 600 DPI minimum for photo-quality, 1200 DPI for fine text.

faqs.question: When do I need white ink for UV printing?
faqs.answer: Transparent substrates (clear acrylic, glass) always need white underbase. Dark materials (black metal, walnut) need white under colored areas. Light substrates (white aluminum, birch) can skip white unless design has light pastels.

faqs.question: What is spot varnish and when should I use it?
faqs.answer: Spot varnish is clear UV ink applied to specific areas for gloss, texture, or protection. Use it on text, logos, or high-touch zones. Multiple passes create raised 3D texture.

faqs.question: Why do my UV prints crack after bending?
faqs.answer: Too much white ink on flexible materials. Reduce white density, use spot white instead of flood white, or switch to a flexible UV ink formulation.

faqs.question: How do I prevent white halos around UV prints?
faqs.answer: Choke the white channel 0.5mm smaller than CMYK layers in your RIP software. This prevents white from showing at edges where layers misalign slightly.

faqs.question: What causes color shifts between materials in UV printing?
faqs.answer: Each material absorbs UV ink differently. Wood grain, metal finish, and acrylic transparency all affect color. Use material-specific ICC profiles and run test prints before production.

title: Embroidery Digitizing Workflow
seoTitle: Embroidery Digitizing Guide — DST/PES Files, Stitch Density, and Pull Compensation
seoDescription: Convert artwork to stitch files for embroidery machines with proper stitch density, underlay, pull compensation, and small text limits.
content:
# Embroidery Digitizing Workflow

Embroidery digitizing converts vector or raster artwork into machine stitch files. Proper digitizing balances detail, stitch count, production speed, and fabric stability. This guide covers the full workflow from artwork to embroidery-ready DST/PES files.

## Why Vectorr for Embroidery?

Auto-Digitizing: Convert logos to stitch paths with automatic stitch direction and density assignment.

Stitch Count Estimator: Preview total stitches and production time before exporting.

Format Converter: Export to DST, PES, JEF, EXP, or any machine-specific format.

## Embroidery File Requirements

1. **Format**: Machine-specific stitch files (DST for industrial, PES for Brother/Babylock, JEF for Janome, EXP for Melco).
2. **Stitch Count**: Most designs 5,000-15,000 stitches. Complex logos can reach 50,000+.
3. **Hoop Size**: Design must fit within machine hoop (typical: 4x4", 5x7", 6x10").
4. **Stitch Density**: 4-6 stitches per mm for satin, 4-5 lines per mm for fill.

## Digitizing Workflow

1. **Clean Artwork**: Simplify paths, remove gradients, consolidate overlapping shapes.
2. **Assign Stitch Types**: Satin for borders/text, fill for large areas, running stitch for outlines.
3. **Set Stitch Direction**: Follow shape contours to minimize puckering.
4. **Add Underlay**: Foundation stitches that stabilize fabric before top stitches.
5. **Apply Pull Compensation**: Expand shapes 0.2-0.4mm to offset fabric compression from needle penetration.
6. **Optimize Stitch Count**: Reduce density in large fills, merge small gaps, eliminate micro-details.

## Stitch Types

**Running Stitch**: Single-line path, used for outlines and fine details. Fastest stitch, minimal thread.

**Satin Stitch**: Zigzag fill that covers shape width. Ideal for borders, letters, and shapes under 10mm wide. Stitch density: 4-6 stitches/mm.

**Fill Stitch**: Parallel lines that cover large areas. Stitch angle follows shape contours. Line spacing: 4-5 lines/mm (0.4-0.5mm apart).

**Tatami Fill**: Standard fill with uniform stitch angle. Used for backgrounds.

**Step Fill**: Fill with staggered start points to reduce fabric push. Better for stretchy fabrics.

## Underlay Strategy

Underlay stitches stabilize fabric before top stitches, preventing registration drift and puckering:

**Center-Line Underlay**: Single running stitch down center of satin column. Minimal coverage, fast.

**Edge-Run Underlay**: Running stitch around perimeter of fill area. Secures edges before fill stitches.

**Zigzag Underlay**: Light satin underlay for wide columns (>5mm). Provides more stability than center-line.

**Fill Underlay**: Light fill at 90° to top fill angle. Essential for large fill areas to prevent fabric movement.

## Pull Compensation

Needle penetration compresses fabric, shrinking the design. Pull compensation expands shapes to offset this:

**Light Fabrics (polo knit, jersey)**: 0.2-0.3mm pull compensation.

**Medium Fabrics (twill, canvas)**: 0.3-0.4mm pull compensation.

**Heavy Fabrics (denim, leather)**: 0.4-0.5mm pull compensation.

**Stretchy Fabrics (spandex, fleece)**: 0.5mm+ pull compensation, plus cutaway stabilizer.

Apply pull compensation globally, then fine-tune narrow columns and small shapes.

## Small Text Limits

**Minimum Height**: 3-4mm for sans-serif, 5mm for serif fonts. Smaller text closes up during stitching.

**Letter Spacing**: Increase 10-20% for small text to prevent overlap.

**Font Choice**: Block fonts (sans-serif, bold) stitch better than script or thin fonts.

**Monogram Fonts**: Designed specifically for embroidery, with built-in spacing and stitch paths.

## Stitch Count Optimization

High stitch counts increase production time, thread breaks, and registration drift. Reduce counts without sacrificing quality:

- Lower fill density from 5 to 4 lines/mm in large areas (backgrounds, fills >500mm²).
- Merge small gaps (<1mm) between shapes into continuous stitches.
- Eliminate details smaller than 1mm (they close up during stitching anyway).
- Use running stitch for outlines instead of narrow satin (<1mm wide).
- Remove hidden stitches (areas covered by overlapping shapes).

## Hoop Size and Placement

**Standard Hoops**: 4x4" (100x100mm), 5x7" (130x180mm), 6x10" (150x260mm).

**Oversized Designs**: Split into multiple hoops with registration marks for alignment.

**Placement**: Mark hoop center on design. Position 50-75mm from collar for shirt logos, center chest for left chest designs.

## Color Changes and Thread Breaks

**Color Sequence**: Minimize color changes to reduce production time. Group same-color elements together.

**Thread Trim**: Set auto-trim for jumps >5mm to prevent long floats on garment back.

**Jump Stitches**: Tie-off and trim between disconnected shapes to avoid thread bridges.

## Common Digitizing Errors

**Puckering**: Too-high stitch density or missing underlay. Reduce density to 4 lines/mm and add edge-run underlay.

**Registration Drift**: Large fills without underlay cause fabric to shift. Add fill underlay at 90° to top stitches.

**Small Text Closes Up**: Text too small (<3mm) or stitch density too high. Increase height or switch to running-stitch font.

**Thread Breaks**: Stitch density too high, thread tension wrong, or needle dull. Reduce density, check tension, replace needle every 8 hours.

**Design Shrinks**: No pull compensation applied. Expand shapes 0.3-0.4mm globally.

title: Vinyl Cutting for Large-Format Signage
seoTitle: Vinyl Cutting for Signage — Weeding, Contour Cuts, and Multi-Panel Alignment
seoDescription: Prepare vinyl cutting files for large-format signage with proper weeding paths, contour cuts, application tape transfer, and multi-panel alignment.
content:
# Vinyl Cutting for Large-Format Signage

Large-format vinyl cutting produces durable outdoor signage, vehicle wraps, and window graphics. Proper file prep ensures clean weeding, accurate contour cuts, and seamless multi-panel alignment. This guide covers the full workflow from design to installed sign.

## Why Vectorr for Vinyl Signage?

Contour Path Generation: Auto-trace complex shapes with offset control for clean cuts.

Weeding Optimization: Automatically identify small islands and bridges that complicate weeding.

Panel Layout: Split large designs across multiple vinyl sheets with alignment marks.

## Vinyl Cutting Requirements

1. **Format**: Vector paths (SVG, PDF, AI, DXF). Raster images must be traced first.
2. **Cut Contour**: Spot-color path (typically named "CutContour" or "Cut") that defines blade path.
3. **Weeding Complexity**: Minimize small islands (<5mm) and narrow bridges (<2mm) for easier weeding.
4. **Vinyl Type**: Cast for outdoor durability (7-10 years), calendered for short-term indoor use (3-5 years).

## Contour Cut Workflow

Contour cutting follows a vector path around printed or solid-color vinyl:

1. **Create Cut Path**: Offset artwork outline by 2-3mm for bleed tolerance.
2. **Assign Spot Color**: Name layer "CutContour" and assign spot color (typically Magenta or a dedicated cut layer).
3. **Simplify Path**: Remove excess anchor points to prevent jagged cuts. Use 0.5-1mm tolerance.
4. **Corner Radius**: Add 1-2mm radius to sharp corners to prevent blade overcut and vinyl tearing.
5. **Registration Marks**: Add crop marks for print-and-cut workflows (printed graphic + contour cut).

## Print-Cut vs Cut-Only

**Cut-Only Vinyl**: Solid-color vinyl (no printing). Cut shape and weed background. Used for decals, lettering, simple logos.

**Print-and-Cut**: Digitally printed vinyl + contour cut. Requires registration marks for cutter to align with printed image. Used for full-color graphics, photographic signage.

## Weeding Strategy

Weeding removes unwanted vinyl after cutting. Complex designs take longer to weed:

**Large Solids**: Fast weeding, minimal complexity.

**Small Islands**: Letters with closed counters (A, O, P) require picking out centers. Minimum 5mm island size for easy weeding.

**Narrow Bridges**: Connecting strokes under 2mm can tear during weeding. Increase stroke width or simplify design.

**Reverse Weeding**: For designs with more solid area than negative space, weed the design itself and keep the background.

## Application Tape Transfer

Application tape (pre-mask) transfers cut vinyl from backing sheet to substrate:

1. **Tape Selection**: Low-tack for delicate surfaces, medium-tack for general use, high-tack for textured surfaces.
2. **Apply Tape**: Roll tape over weeded vinyl, squeegee from center outward to eliminate bubbles.
3. **Peel Backing**: Slowly peel vinyl backing sheet away, leaving vinyl stuck to tape.
4. **Position on Substrate**: Align tape+vinyl on target surface, squeegee from center outward.
5. **Remove Tape**: Peel tape at 45° angle, leaving vinyl adhered to substrate.

## Multi-Panel Alignment

Large signs (vehicle wraps, building graphics) span multiple vinyl panels. Accurate alignment is critical:

**Overlap Method**: Design panels with 10-20mm overlap. Install first panel, then overlay second panel and trim overlap with blade.

**Butt-Join Method**: Design panels edge-to-edge with no overlap. Requires precise cutter registration and installation. Use alignment marks every 500mm.

**Registration Marks**: Add crosshairs at panel corners (10mm from edge) on every panel. Match marks during installation.

**Panel Numbering**: Label each panel with position (A1, A2, B1, B2) for correct assembly sequence.

## Outdoor Durability

**Cast Vinyl**: Conforms to curves, 7-10 year outdoor life. Used for vehicle wraps, permanent signage.

**Calendered Vinyl**: Flat surfaces only, 3-5 year outdoor life. Budget option for short-term signage.

**Lamination**: Add clear laminate over printed vinyl to protect from UV, scratches, and graffiti. Gloss, matte, or textured finishes available.

**Surface Prep**: Clean substrate with isopropyl alcohol, remove wax/grease, dry completely before application.

## Blade Settings

**Blade Depth**: Cut through vinyl and adhesive, kiss-cut the backing. Test cut should peel vinyl cleanly without cutting backing.

**Blade Force**: Too light = incomplete cuts, too heavy = backing tears and blade dulls faster. Start at 80-120g force, adjust per material.

**Speed**: Slower for intricate designs (10-20 cm/s), faster for simple shapes (40-60 cm/s).

**Blade Type**: 45° for general vinyl, 60° for thick materials, 30° for fine detail.

## Common Vinyl Cutting Issues

**Jagged Edges**: Blade dull or too much force. Replace blade every 500-1000m of cutting, reduce force 10-20%.

**Vinyl Not Cutting Through**: Blade depth too shallow or force too low. Increase depth by 0.1mm increments until clean cut achieved.

**Backing Paper Torn**: Blade depth too deep. Reduce depth until kiss-cut (vinyl cuts, backing stays intact).

**Weeding Tears Vinyl**: Design too intricate or blade corners too sharp. Simplify design, add corner radius, reduce force.

**Bubbles During Application**: Squeegee technique incorrect. Apply from center outward in overlapping strokes, 45° angle, firm pressure.

title: Laser Engraving Production File Setup
seoTitle: Laser Engraving File Prep — Vector vs Raster, Power/Speed, and Kerf Offset
seoDescription: Prepare files for CO2 and fiber laser engraving with vector cutting vs raster engraving, power/speed tuning, kerf offset for inlays, and focus height.
content:
# Laser Engraving Production File Setup

Laser cutting and engraving use focused light to vaporize material. CO2 lasers work on wood, acrylic, leather, and fabric; fiber lasers mark metal. Proper file prep separates vector cuts from raster engraving, tunes power/speed per material, and applies kerf offset for press-fit joints. This guide covers the full production workflow.

## Why Vectorr for Laser Production?

Vector vs Raster Layer Separation: Assign cut paths to one layer, engravings to another for automatic job routing.

Kerf Offset Calculation: Shrink or expand cut paths to compensate for laser beam width.

Material Library: Load power/speed/frequency presets for wood, acrylic, leather, metal, and more.

## Laser File Requirements

1. **Format**: Vector paths (SVG, PDF, AI, DXF) for cutting, raster images (PNG, JPG) for engraving.
2. **Cut Path**: Hairline stroke (0.001" or "Hairline" in software) on a dedicated layer (typically red or "CutContour").
3. **Engrave Layer**: Black fill for raster engraving, or vector fill for vector engraving (slower but more consistent).
4. **Kerf Offset**: Beam width compensation for press-fit parts (typically 0.1-0.2mm per side).

## Vector Cutting vs Raster Engraving

**Vector Cutting**: Laser follows path outline, cuts through material. Used for shapes, parts, stencils. Fast, precise edges.

**Raster Engraving**: Laser scans back and forth like a printer, removing surface material. Used for photos, text, textures. Slower, variable depth.

**Vector Engraving**: Laser follows path outline but doesn't cut through. Used for line art, borders, hatching. Faster than raster for simple shapes.

## Power, Speed, and Frequency

Every material requires specific settings. Too much power = charring; too little = incomplete cuts.

**Power (%)**: Laser wattage output. Higher power cuts thicker materials or engraves deeper.

**Speed (mm/s or in/s)**: How fast laser head moves. Slower = more energy per area = deeper cut/engrave.

**Frequency (Hz or PPI)**: Pulse rate. Higher frequency = smoother edges on wood, lower = deeper engraving on acrylic.

### Common Material Settings (40W CO2 Laser)

**3mm Plywood**: Cut at 20mm/s, 80% power, 500Hz. Engrave at 300mm/s, 30% power, 1000Hz.

**3mm Acrylic**: Cut at 10mm/s, 70% power, 5000Hz. Engrave at 400mm/s, 40% power, 5000Hz.

**3mm MDF**: Cut at 15mm/s, 90% power, 500Hz. Engrave at 250mm/s, 25% power, 1000Hz.

**Leather (2mm)**: Cut at 40mm/s, 50% power, 1000Hz. Engrave at 500mm/s, 20% power, 1000Hz.

**Cardboard (corrugated)**: Cut at 60mm/s, 40% power, 500Hz.

Higher-wattage lasers (60W, 100W, 150W) use proportionally lower power percentages for the same material.

## Kerf Offset for Press-Fit Joints

Kerf is the width of material removed by the laser beam (typically 0.1-0.3mm). For press-fit parts (box joints, puzzle pieces, inlays), compensate kerf to achieve tight tolerance:

**Male Parts (tabs)**: Shrink outline by half the kerf (e.g., 0.1mm offset inward).

**Female Parts (slots)**: Expand outline by half the kerf (e.g., 0.1mm offset outward).

**Inlays**: Expand the inlay pocket by full kerf (0.2mm) so the insert drops in snugly.

Test kerf on scrap material first — every laser and material combination has slightly different kerf width.

## Focus Height and Air Assist

**Focus Height**: Distance from lens to material surface. Incorrect focus = wide kerf, poor edge quality, incomplete cuts. Focal point should sit at material top surface for cutting, mid-thickness for engraving.

**Air Assist**: Compressed air blown at cut point to remove smoke and prevent charring. Essential for clean cuts on wood and acrylic. Turn off for paper (air blows it around).

## Layer Organization

Separate cut paths and engraving areas by layer or color:

**Red (or CutContour layer)**: Vector cuts, highest power, slowest speed. Runs last to prevent parts from shifting.

**Black (or Engrave layer)**: Raster or vector engraving, medium power, fast speed. Runs first.

**Blue (or Score layer)**: Light vector engraving for fold lines, medium power, medium speed.

Laser software reads colors/layers and assigns different power/speed to each.

## Multi-Pass Cutting

Thick materials (>6mm wood, >10mm acrylic) require multiple passes:

**Pass 1**: 80% power, 15mm/s.

**Pass 2**: 90% power, 12mm/s.

**Pass 3**: 95% power, 10mm/s (if needed).

Lower power on first pass prevents excessive charring. Increase power on later passes to push through remaining material.

## Safety and Material Restrictions

**Never laser cut**: PVC (releases chlorine gas), vinyl (toxic), polycarbonate (melts and releases cyanide), fiberglass (releases glass dust), any material containing chlorine or fluorine.

**Safe materials**: Wood, plywood, MDF, acrylic (cast, not extruded), leather (vegetable-tanned, not chrome-tanned), paper, cardboard, fabric (cotton, polyester), glass (CO2 etching only), anodized aluminum (fiber laser).

## Common Laser Issues

**Charred Edges**: Power too high, speed too slow, or insufficient air assist. Reduce power 10%, increase speed 20%, verify air compressor pressure.

**Incomplete Cuts**: Power too low, speed too fast, or focus height incorrect. Increase power or reduce speed, check focus with calibration tool.

**Wavy Cut Lines**: Laser head loose, belts slack, or lens dirty. Tighten belts, clean lens with isopropyl alcohol and lens paper.

**Flame-Polished Edges (acrylic)**: Correct. Acrylic melts and self-polishes when laser-cut. To prevent, use masking tape on both sides before cutting.

title: CNC Router Toolpath Generation
seoTitle: CNC Router Toolpath Guide — Climb vs Conventional, Step-Over, and Tab Placement
seoDescription: Generate CNC router toolpaths from vectors with climb vs conventional milling, step-over percentage, tab placement, Z-zero methods, and feed rates.
content:
# CNC Router Toolpath Generation

CNC routers cut shapes from sheet goods (plywood, MDF, aluminum) using rotating end mills. Toolpath generation converts vector outlines and 3D models into G-code machine instructions. This guide covers climb vs conventional milling, step-over, tab placement, Z-zero, and feed rates for efficient, accurate production.

## Why Vectorr for CNC Routing?

Automatic Toolpath Generation: Convert vector paths to G-code with climb/conventional selection and offset compensation.

Tab Placement Preview: Visualize where tabs hold parts in place before cutting.

Feed Rate Calculator: Optimize speed and RPM per material and bit diameter.

## CNC Router File Requirements

1. **Input Format**: Vector paths (DXF, SVG, AI) for 2D profiles, STL or STEP for 3D carving.
2. **Output Format**: G-code (machine instructions) or tool-specific format (e.g., .sbp for ShopBot, .nc for generic CNC).
3. **Tool Library**: End mill diameter, flute count, material (HSS, carbide, compression).
4. **Material Thickness**: Exact measurement for depth calculations and tab placement.

## Climb Milling vs Conventional Milling

The direction the bit rotates relative to feed direction affects surface finish and tool life:

**Climb Milling (Down-Cut)**: Bit rotates in same direction as feed. Chip load starts thick, ends thin.

- **Pros**: Smoother finish, less chipout on top edge, less tool deflection.
- **Cons**: Can pull part loose if not secured, requires rigid machine.
- **Use for**: Final pass on visible edges, hardwoods, aluminum.

**Conventional Milling (Up-Cut)**: Bit rotates opposite to feed direction. Chip load starts thin, ends thick.

- **Pros**: Better chip evacuation, less likely to pull part loose.
- **Cons**: Rougher finish, more chipout on top edge.
- **Use for**: Roughing passes, softwoods, plastics.

**Best Practice**: Rough cuts in conventional, final pass in climb for best finish.

## Step-Over and Depth of Cut

**Step-Over**: Overlap percentage between adjacent tool passes. Smaller step-over = smoother finish but longer cut time.

- **Roughing**: 40-60% of bit diameter (faster, rougher).
- **Finishing**: 10-30% of bit diameter (slower, smoother).
- **3D Carving**: 5-15% for fine detail.

**Depth of Cut**: How deep the bit plunges per pass. Depends on material hardness and bit diameter.

- **Softwood (pine, poplar)**: 50-100% of bit diameter per pass.
- **Hardwood (oak, maple)**: 25-50% of bit diameter per pass.
- **MDF**: 50-75% of bit diameter per pass.
- **Aluminum**: 10-30% of bit diameter per pass, use cutting fluid.
- **Acrylic**: 30-50% of bit diameter, single-flute bit to prevent melting.

## Tab Placement

Tabs are small uncut sections that hold parts in place during cutting:

**Tab Size**: 3-6mm wide, 50-75% of material thickness. Larger parts need bigger tabs.

**Tab Count**: Minimum 3 tabs per part, 4+ for parts over 300mm. Space evenly around perimeter.

**Tab Location**: Place on straight edges or gentle curves, never on tight inside corners (stress concentrator). Avoid placing tabs where surface finish matters.

**Tab Cleanup**: Sand, chisel, or router after cutting. Leave 1-2mm tab material and sand flush.

## Z-Zero Methods

Z-zero sets the vertical reference point for depth calculations:

**Material Top**: Zero probe touches material surface. Use for through-cuts and profiles. Easy to reset between parts.

**Spoilboard Top**: Zero probe touches waste board under material. Use for pocketing and engraving where material thickness varies. Requires precise material thickness measurement.

**Tool Length Offset**: Machine stores tool lengths, auto-adjusts Z-zero when changing bits. Professional machines only.

Always re-zero Z after changing bits or material.

## Feed Rate and RPM

**Feed Rate**: How fast the bit moves through material (mm/min or in/min). Too fast = rough finish and bit breakage. Too slow = burning and dull bit.

**RPM**: Spindle rotation speed. Higher RPM for small bits and soft materials, lower RPM for large bits and hard materials.

**Chip Load**: Amount of material removed per tooth per revolution. Optimal chip load depends on material and bit type.

### General Feed Rate Formula

Feed Rate (mm/min) = RPM × Number of Flutes × Chip Load (mm)

**Example**: 1/4" 2-flute carbide in MDF
- RPM: 18,000
- Flutes: 2
- Chip Load: 0.1mm
- Feed Rate: 18,000 × 2 × 0.1 = 3,600 mm/min (141 in/min)

### Common Material Settings (1/4" carbide bit)

**MDF/Plywood**: 18,000 RPM, 3,000-4,500 mm/min feed, 6mm depth of cut.

**Hardwood**: 16,000 RPM, 2,000-3,000 mm/min feed, 4mm depth of cut.

**Softwood**: 18,000 RPM, 4,000-6,000 mm/min feed, 8mm depth of cut.

**Aluminum**: 12,000 RPM, 800-1,500 mm/min feed, 2mm depth of cut, flood coolant.

**Acrylic**: 10,000 RPM, 2,000-3,000 mm/min feed, 5mm depth of cut, single-flute bit.

## Bit Selection

**Straight Bit**: Flat end, used for profiles, pockets, dados. Most common.

**Ball Nose**: Rounded end, used for 3D carving and contoured surfaces.

**V-Bit**: Angled tip, used for engraving text, V-carve inlays, chamfers.

**Compression Bit**: Up-cut flutes at bottom, down-cut at top. Clean edges on both surfaces. Best for plywood.

**Downcut Bit**: Pushes chips down, clean top edge. Use for through-cuts where top surface matters.

**Upcut Bit**: Pulls chips up, clean bottom edge. Better chip evacuation for deep cuts.

## Common CNC Routing Errors

**Bit Breakage**: Feed rate too high, depth of cut too deep, or bit dull. Reduce feed rate 20-30%, shallow depth of cut, replace bit.

**Rough Finish**: Wrong milling direction (use climb for final pass), dull bit, or excessive step-over. Use sharp carbide bit, reduce step-over to 25%.

**Part Pulled Loose**: Insufficient tabs, climb milling on unsecured part, or tabs too small. Add more tabs, increase tab size, use conventional milling.

**Burning**: Feed rate too slow or RPM too high. Increase feed rate 20-30%, reduce RPM 10-20%.

**Chipout on Top Edge**: Conventional milling on final pass, or dull bit. Use climb milling for final pass, use compression bit for plywood.

faqs.question: What is the difference between climb and conventional milling?
faqs.answer: Climb milling rotates the bit in the feed direction (smoother finish, less chipout, better for final passes). Conventional milling rotates opposite to feed (better chip evacuation, rougher finish, safer for roughing).

faqs.question: How many tabs do I need for CNC cutting?
faqs.answer: Minimum 3 tabs per part, 4+ for parts over 300mm. Space evenly on straight edges or gentle curves. Tab size: 3-6mm wide, 50-75% material thickness.

faqs.question: What causes CNC bits to break?
faqs.answer: Feed rate too high, depth of cut too deep, or dull bit. Reduce feed rate 20-30%, limit depth to 50% of bit diameter (hardwood) or 100% (softwood), replace bit if cutting poorly.

faqs.question: Should I zero my CNC router to material top or spoilboard?
faqs.answer: Material top for through-cuts and profiles (easier to reset between parts). Spoilboard top for pockets and engraving (handles varying material thickness). Always re-zero after changing bits.

faqs.question: How do I calculate CNC feed rate?
faqs.answer: Feed Rate = RPM × Flutes × Chip Load. Example: 18,000 RPM, 2-flute bit, 0.1mm chip load = 3,600 mm/min. Adjust down 20-30% for harder materials.
